title: The boat, the boy, the wall
hookLine: each strange act has a hidden mercy Musa couldn't see (18:71–82)
last: YOU WON'T BE ABLE TO BE PATIENT.

cards: Musa has promised to ask nothing. A boat's crew recognizes al-Khidr and lets them both ride for free. The moment they're aboard, al-Khidr takes a tool and knocks a hole in the boat.
Musa forgets his promise: you've made a hole to drown its people? Al-Khidr says, quietly: didn't I tell you you couldn't be patient? That's the first of three.

teach.h: THE BOAT: A KING WHO SEIZES SHIPS.
teach.b: Musa apologizes: don't blame me for forgetting. They go on. They meet a boy, and al-Khidr kills him.
Musa is horrified, and says so: you've killed an innocent soul. Second warning. They come to a town, hungry, and ask for food.
The people refuse them. In that town a wall is about to fall down, and al-Khidr rebuilds it. Musa says: you could at least have charged them for it.

And al-Khidr says: this is where we part. Then he explains. The boat belonged to poor people who worked the sea, and a king ahead was seizing every sound boat by force; a damaged boat would be left alone.
The boy, he says, would have pressed his believing parents into rebellion and disbelief, and God would give them a better child in his place.
The wall stood over a treasure belonging to two orphan boys whose father had been a righteous man, and God wanted them to grow up and dig it out themselves.
Then the line, in Pickthall's words: "I did it not upon my own command."

teach.h: THE BOY: A FUTURE ONLY GOD KNEW.
teach.b: Muslim scholars are clear about the second scene: al-Khidr acted on direct command from God, about a future only God knew, and no person may take it as permission for harm.
The law forbids it. The story isn't teaching people to act on hidden reasons.

teach.h: A BIRD'S SIP FROM THE SEA.
teach.b: It's teaching what it's like to watch from inside a story you can't see the end of.

teach.h: I DID IT NOT UPON MY OWN COMMAND.
teach.b: Bukhari's hadith adds two details: a small bird dipped its beak in the sea, and al-Khidr said their knowledge beside God's was like that sip beside the ocean.
And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: we wish Musa had been patient, so we could have been told more.

how: Muslims read 18:71–82 as a lesson in trusting God's wisdom in hardship, while scholars stress that al-Khidr's acts were by special divine command and are never a precedent for anyone to cause harm.

o: holed to save it from a king who seized ships
the ark that carried Musa to the two seas
sunk to punish a crew who wouldn't pay

games.q: the three acts, and the reasons — tap the pairs.
p: a king seizing every sound ship

s: the town welcomed them with food
the people refused them hospitality, and al-Khidr rebuilt their wall anyway.
scholars treat al-Khidr's acts as a model anyone may follow
they stress he acted on direct command from God; the law forbids harm on hidden reasons.
the Prophet wished Musa had been more patient
so that more of their story could have been told (Bukhari).

games.q: a town has refused you food. you see their wall about to collapse, and your companion rebuilds it for free. what do you say, as Musa?
o: you could at least have charged them for it.
games.why: Musa says he could have taken a wage, his third question, and al-Khidr says: this is where we part. then he explains all three.

practice: Bring to mind a setback from your past that felt like a hole knocked in your boat: a job you didn't get, a move you didn't want, a door that shut.
With some years between you and it, look again for anything that came because of it, unseen back then. If you find one, hold it; if you don't, that's honest too, since some reasons stay hidden.

wordCard.voice: The boat. Holed to save it from a king, the first of three acts that looked wrong to Musa and turned out to hide a mercy. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: there was a reason. Not every reason is ours to see. That's day four hundred sixty-nine.

sources.q: I did it not upon my own command.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 122, 4725 (the bird's beak; we wish Musa had been patient)
